headline: Danbury officials condemn masked white-supremacist rally outside police headquarters
dek: Police say they learned of the brief Oct. 3 demonstration only after it ended; the gathering followed Danbury’s vote to open police applications to lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients.
body: A masked group carrying a “Keep New England White” banner demonstrated outside Danbury police headquarters Saturday night, prompting condemnations from city and state officials and a statement from the police chief. The gathering was documented in video and confirmed by Danbury police after the group had left, according to the Stamford Advocate’s Oct. 5 report: https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/article/white-supremacist-group-danbury-police-22462288.php.

The video showed roughly a dozen people on a public sidewalk near the department, some wearing face coverings. Local reporting said people in the group could be heard shouting white-supremacist slogans and making Nazi-style salutes. Police spokesperson Erin Henry told the Stamford Advocate that officers were not aware of the demonstration while it was happening and had no interaction with the participants. Chief Patrick Ridenhour said the department confirmed the footage was authentic and stressed that the demonstrators were not police employees.

Ridenhour said the department cannot control who uses a public sidewalk outside its building, but he rejected the group’s message as inconsistent with the department’s mission. He said Danbury police do not support or condone organizations that promote hate or exclusion and are committed to protecting everyone in the city. The police department had not announced arrests or criminal charges in the reporting available Monday, and the length of the demonstration was not clear.

Mayor Roberto Alves said Danbury has no place for hate, racism or white supremacy and described the city’s racial, religious and cultural diversity as a strength. In an interview with public-radio station WSHU, Alves said the participants appeared to arrive briefly and disperse quickly, and that police were investigating. WSHU’s report, published Oct. 5, also included the perspective of Carolina Bortoletto of Danbury United for Immigrants, who said the demonstration was intended to frighten an immigrant community: https://www.wshu.org/connecticut-news/2026-10-05/ct-danbury-mayor-white-power-rally.

The demonstration came weeks after the Danbury City Council voted 18-2 to change the eligibility rules for police applicants. The ordinance now permits lawful permanent residents and recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, to apply. The change did not remove the department’s other screening requirements, including background, medical, psychological, physical and drug testing. The city’s published ordinance says applicants must also complete the required Connecticut police training and pass a competitive civil-service process: https://www.danbury-ct.gov/DocumentCenter/View/6916/Meeting-Notice-and-Packet---PD-Ordinances-Sec-22-19-thru-22-30--42826?bidId=.

The timing and stated target of the rally were reported by Danbury Patch, which said Northeast Action claimed responsibility in a Telegram post and connected the demonstration to the council’s hiring decision. Patch also reported that the Counter Extremism Project has described Northeast Action as a neo-Nazi organization and said the group claims activity across Connecticut and other Northeastern states. Those descriptions come from the reporting and outside group assessments; NorthEast News has not independently verified the organization’s membership or the authenticity of every online post: https://patch.com/connecticut/danbury/neo-nazi-group-targets-danbury-after-police-hiring-change.

The incident has raised a local question that extends beyond one brief protest: how public agencies protect free expression in public spaces while responding to intimidation aimed at residents or public employees. Danbury officials have condemned the message, but the available reports do not describe arrests, injuries or property damage. The city and police have not publicly identified participants, and it remains unclear whether the investigation will produce any charges or additional public-safety measures.

For residents, the immediate facts are limited but clear. The demonstration occurred outside the police headquarters on Oct. 3, police learned of it after it ended, officials confirmed the video and publicly rejected the group’s message. Any further response will depend on what investigators can establish about the participants, their conduct and whether any law was violated.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoDescription: Danbury police and officials responded after a masked group demonstrated outside police headquarters following a vote to expand police applicant eligibility.
